Chapter 9: Finding Home in Unexpected Places
As this family’s story unfolds, the meaning of home keeps changing, doesn’t it? For anyone who’s crossed borders and started fresh, home isn’t really about a single place—it’s more of a feeling. It’s that sense of belonging you can create wherever people gather, especially when you’re sharing a meal.
Picture this: a daughter, now living far from where she grew up, invites her friends over for dinner. She spends her afternoon in the kitchen, making those dishes she remembers from childhood. Sometimes she has to improvise, laugh at her own mistakes, and make do with ingredients that aren’t quite the same. Still, the act of cooking somehow brings her closer to the family she misses so much. Her friends are curious, asking about the flavors, and the stories behind every dish. Before she knows it, she’s retelling the same tales her parents once shared, realizing she’s become the keeper of her family’s history.
Meanwhile, in another city, her brother is starting his own family. He teaches his kids how to make rice just right, how to taste for salt, and how to listen for that special sizzle that means the tahdig is ready. Their kitchen turns into this amazing place of connection—a bridge between generations and cultures. At first, the kids might not really care, but over time, those little rituals start to mean something. What once seemed strange becomes a comforting tradition.
So, here’s the key: home isn’t a fixed place—it’s a practice. It’s something we build and rebuild, one meal and one story at a time. A lot of us try to find home in our memories, but for families living between cultures, home is always a work in progress. The kitchen—no matter where it is—becomes a kind of sanctuary. It’s where the past and present come together, where family bonds are renewed, and where the search for belonging keeps going.
